utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, before re-examination begins, I seek leave to ask to reopen cross-examination for the purposes of asking just a few questions of this witness. Can I explain the context? With witnesses of this kind, Pauk is always a very major influence in when cross-examination should conclude. As I indicated last week, a whole range of issues were necessarily dropped because there was never going to be time. On review, it looked as though there may have been about three topics which can all be susceptible to basically about one question, or two questions each, where it would probably be fair to join issue with the witness and to explain what the Prosecution's position on those very short topics are. I'll explain what they relate to. The first meeting of the witness with the accused, the conduct of Seselj's men, which he said was always proper, and the training camps at Bubanj Potok and Golubic and to whom they were responsive. But each of them is a very short topic. Before I invite the Chamber to decide on my application, can I make this point as well: This witness made a range of observations about people who had been witnesses in the case, Vasiljevic, Dulovic, Anastasijevic, amongst others, I think, which were not put to those witnesses. In some cases, it's been possible to have reactions from the witnesses, although not to explore those reactions in full, again for want of time. My present intention in respect of those matters that were advanced in evidence and are now the subject of response from those witnesses is to put the responses in the form of 92 bis statements and to serve them for consideration as rebuttal. But where matters of -- the matters raised against Vasiljevic were very serious. They weren't put to him in detail or I think sometimes simply at all in cross-examination. And the Chamber may decide in due course that it's appropriate to have that material before it in the form of rebuttal. But that's part of the topic. The real request at the moment is to be asked -- to be granted leave to ask probably about half a dozen questions, one of which would involve looking at one of the extracts from the witness's book, which I actually thought I had put in, but I'm assured I hadn't. But it wouldn't take very long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll consider it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, any comments on this?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I have nothing against Mr. Nice asking questions which he omitted to ask in the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Nice. We'll allow you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm much obliged and I shall be extremely brief. If we can first of all distribute the one document from the writings of the witness that I'd like him to look at. It relates to his account --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Nice: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, this relates to your account of your first encounter with the accused which you've said was in 1992, April or May of 1992, you said was purely formal in its context. Would you look, please, at this extract from your book, "Serbian Ceausescu Couple," published in 1995. And if you'd be good enough, please, to go in the original-language version, your page 158, you'll see two sidelined passages.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And if the Chamber would be good enough to look at the English-language version, if they still have the document. It's 46 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: What's the tab?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- in the list.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: What is the tab number, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We see the two sidelined passages marked, say the following. The first one says: "Milosevic stood up and said it's an honour to meet you. On my behalf I said my respects, Mr. President. We shook hands and I immediately went further." And then further down the page, relating to the same event which we can see, I think, is chronicled by you as May 1992, you say: "Milosevic asked us, the Radicals, to send more volunteers across the Drina, and in exchange, promised adequate supplies of arms, uniforms, and means of transport. This collaboration worked well until September 1993." Mr. Seselj, is the position that your first meeting with this accused was not just formality but involved his requesting you to send volunteers in exchange for arms?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. Nice, you didn't understand the text itself. This is a question of two meetings here. The first meeting is the one that I described in detail, in April 1992, at a meeting of the National Assembly, or popular Assembly, at which Mr. Milosevic was present sitting in the first row when I arrived. So it was just a matter of shaking hands. However, there's a remark here which you omitted to read out, which follows on immediately after what you said. It said: "Members of the Socialist Party of Serbia, even from the closest leadership were convinced that for a long time we were having meetings at all political moves I was making in direct agreement with their leader." You see, here we're talking about a mystification that's going on. This really was the held opinion of the public, what the public thought. And many newspapers wrote about it as well. Usually of the opposition regime. However, all the conclusions were drawn from one single fact, and that is that by having been elected national deputy, as the only deputy of the Serbian Radical Party in the National Assembly, that I quite literally, in the verbal duels, toppled the whole of the pro-western opposition. That's the first point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We can have the whole passage translated, of course. But even if your first encounters were split as between April and May, and it may be elsewhere in this book, you put it at 1991, but nevertheless, stay with 1992, is it right that at the main meeting, so a very early meeting, you were asked to send volunteers in exchange for arms?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't say 1991 anywhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it right that you were asked to send volunteers in exchange for arms and uniforms and means of transport?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not correct. Because at that meeting, we only discussed the forthcoming federal elections. However, you must have -- you ought to have given the Trial Chamber the full information. What does this text represent? Let's look at that first. Take a look at the title of this text, to begin with. In the title it says the following: "I dream every night that they are executing Sloba Mira on Dedinje and how Desimir Tosic is being eaten by a viper -- wild boar." This is the text that I wrote in the central prison in Belgrade while I was there for four months, and I took it out of the prison illegally and published it in the Novi Sad Svet newspaper. And I insist that the introductory part of this text be read out and then everything will be clear to one and all. It's just half a page, Mr. Robinson, if you have nothing against me doing that, and then things will be quite clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As far as I'm concerned, I've achieved the purpose I want, which is to have the recording of what's on the page that we've looked at, the second of the two extracts. Other matters could probably be a matter for re-examination. I'm quite content that the passage that the witness wants dealt with can be the subject of translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, we would not have you read that. The accused may re-examine you in relation to that part.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm much obliged.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, the second thing I want to ask about is this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May this document be admitted, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be 920.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The second point I want to ask you about is this: You've spoken in general terms about the behaviour of your Seselj's men. A witness before this Court, C-57 of the JNA, who fought alongside your men, gave evidence to the following effect, and I'll summarise it in five phrases: That they didn't recognise the authority of commanding officers; that they were a gang of thugs; that they looted when in Luzac; that one of their number cut off the ear of a prisoner, or both ears of a prisoner in Luzac; and that then, later, in the course of the exercise at Vukovar and at the surrender of Borovo Komerc shelter, Seselj's men were seen to be or calculated to be cutting off fingers, to rob corpses of jewellery, and to extract teeth from mouths, and were seen at that site to be beating men. So those are the allegations specifically made against Seselj's men by a witness in this case, C-57. Do you have any comment on that? Are those allegations true or may they be true?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those are terrible fabrications. And many of your false witnesses try and do that. The members of my expert team warned me because I couldn't see it clearly on the screen in front of me, but they warned me that that alleged soldier, the JNA soldier who gave you the statement on the piece of footage that you've shown and spoke about Virovitica, Ogulin, that border, had his wedding ring on his left hand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... is a protected witness, so, Mr. Seselj, be careful before you say anything that has the purpose or the effect of allowing any part of recognition by others of -- identification of others of whom he is. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, you heard that. The witness is protected, so don't say anything that would reveal his identity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I think the witness is referring to the video clip we had last Friday of the film in Vukovar, and the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Spoke in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no intention of disclosing the protected witness, nor do I know the name of that witness. The witness is just a code number for me. I'm saying that his testimony was false. Now, the fact that I say that his testimony is false does not mean that the whole of Serbia will recognise him as being a liar and saying that's probably the one, he's a liar, he's telling terrible lies. Secondly, the soldier who was shown here is wearing, as I said, his wedding ring on his left hand. A wedding ring is a ring which symbolically shows that somebody is married, has entered into matrimony, a man or a woman. With Orthodox Serbs, that ring always, in all cases, is exclusively worn on the right hand. Now, the fact that that soldier had his wedding ring, wedding band on his left hand says that he's not a Orthodox Serb, that he is a Catholic or something else. And secondly, it is absolutely impossible for a JNA unit to have marched through Vukovar in the way that those people marched after the liberation of Vukovar, except if that was improvised by somebody for the purposes of the television camera and having it filmed. That's what I wanted to say. And secondly, if it's true that someone's ears had been cut off and that person survived having had his ears cut off, then it is very easy to find that Croat or Muslim who the Seselj men allegedly cut off his ears and bring him into court and show him. And then he can say: "My ears were cut off by so-and-so." This is just imagination, everything fabricated, that they cut fingers off corpses. When post-mortems were conducted, one would be able to see whether teeth were extracted or fingers cut off. These are all stories dating back to World War II and the things that the Ustashas did to the Serbs during World War II.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speaker kindly be asked to slow down, thank you, for the benefit of one and all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, thank you, and the interpreters are asking you to slow down for the benefit of one and all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Clarification, Mr. Seselj. The person you say had the wedding ring on the left hand, was that the person who was speaking in the English language or was it one of the others?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was that alleged Chetnik of yours who spoke English.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, the witness has connected the conduct alleged through C-57 with what was on the screen, but he hasn't necessarily answered the question. But I've given him a chance to do so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And my last question relates to the two training camps that you say your men were trained at, Bubanj Potok and Golubic. It's right, isn't it, that Bubanj Potok was never a JNA camp; it was a DB camp under the MUP; and that Golubic in Knin was a training camp where Captain Dragan operated. So that neither of these training camps was in fact a JNA camp; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not correct. First of all, in Bubanj Potok, as far as I know, there was never any training there. Bubanj Potok was exclusively a JNA barracks, and that was the collection point for the volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party. That is where the volunteers went, that is where they received their war deployment papers, their uniforms. Sometimes weapons, but not always. And then they were driven to the front, where they were most needed. Now, as far as the camp in Golubic, the training camp in Golubic was concerned, I was never there, I have to say. But I don't think that that was within the frameworks of the JNA but the police of Srpksa Krajina. But I'm not sure about that. I don't have any set information about that. Because I know that the JNA officers were very much against Captain Dragan because of his bombastic statements made to the public that he tried to interfere in their affairs and business. And Captain Dragan, at the request of JNA officers, was dismissed from Knin, sent out of Knin, before the combat had actually finished. And he returned subsequently in November to topple Milan Babic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've made the points I wish to make.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I answered your first question as well by asserting that it was a complete fabrication, that statement made by your witness, what did you say, C-65 or whatever. It is a terrible falsehood.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I've made the point, so that I can now honourably present the points in closing arguments. And one other point that I meant to raise last week is this -- with the Chamber. The Chamber has had a large number of extracts from the interview of this witness with the makers of the Death of Yugoslavia film. For the most part, they're not taken from the film; they're taken from the interview itself. The full transcript of that interview is of course available, as is I think the interview itself. We know that the transcript provided by the makers of the film would, before being really acceptable here, require retranslation. But it occurs to us that it might be helpful for the Chamber, I make this application, to have the whole of that transcript available, subject, of course, to it being properly interpreted or translated by CLSS here. I've tried to extract from it points that are of particular pertinence and value at this stage, but there may well be other points that will become relevant and of value, and for that reason, it's my submission that the whole of the tape, in light of the large number of parts that have already gone in, will be of assistance to you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I think that that request is unacceptable. Mr. Nice had the possibility of showing the witness portions and extracts which he considered to be relevant. And the witness, and that is fair play towards the witness, then has the opportunity of explaining what he's been asked and give a response and answer. What Mr. Nice is now asking is to have the transcript of the interview admitted, which was not shown the witness and to which the witness has no possibility of making a response or giving any kind of explanation. And I consider that to be unacceptable. If Mr. Nice wishes to tender into evidence other extracts from the transcript, let him show them to the witness, let him put them to the witness and ask him questions. Because the question arises of why he showed portions of the transcript if he didn't indeed expect an answer from the witness. But I think that he doesn't like the responses and answers he has been given, and then he's trying to have the transcript admitted without giving the witness an opportunity of answering what he is showing. That is highly improper and I'm against having anything admitted into evidence which was not put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We consider, Mr. Milosevic, that there is merit in your response. The motion is refused.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm grateful to the Chamber for allowing me to ask those additional questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, re-examination to continue. I have to say, Mr. Milosevic, that I understand Mr. Delic is waiting anxiously in the wings to resume his testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That's what I understood. So I'll do my best to be as expeditious as possible. Unfortunately, I do still have a number of questions which I cannot drop. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Re-examined by Mr. Milosevic: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, over the past few days, including this morning's session, you have provided an explanation of the reasons and the emphasis of your statements and the contents of your statements against me and against my wife. I'm not going to go back to that, because I consider that you have explained that sufficiently. Now, my question to you is this: Bearing in mind all the statements you made over all the years that you mentioned and were mentioned indeed by Mr. Nice himself, my question is this: What kind of relationship did we have, the relationship between us, and what did these statements and attacks testify to? Were relations as tense as Mr. Nice was showing here for days? Did it allow us to have any kind of relationship or any kind of conspiracy, or did our relationships, as they stood, exclude any possibility of that kind?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: They absolutely excluded any such possibility. Our relationship, from 1993 and the whole of 1994, 1995, 1996, 1997, were the relationship of open hostility. There was open hostility between us. Constant conflicts in which nobody minded what they said in this battle. Of course, you didn't take part in those conflicts. You tried to avoid them. And I don't think you ever uttered my name in public in all those years. But that is why your people, your men, the men from your party, the high-ranking functionaries, did take part in that conflict and clash, and in fact it was through them that I attacked you as the party leader, you being the party leader and the number-one man of the regime. So it is quite impossible that there was any conspiracy or collaboration between us, and collusion, because we didn't even know each other before those years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A moment ago, you quoted the excerpt that Mr. Nice had failed to quote, where it says that members of the Socialist Party, even the closest leadership, were convinced that we had been meeting for a long time previously. But you didn't go on to quote the end of that paragraph and the last sentence, in fact, where it says: "And actually, there were no indirect contacts either."

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. No contacts whatsoever, of any kind. However, there was an intrigue in 1991 when I won all out at the additional elections for the National Assembly in Rakovica, by winning more votes than all the other candidates put together. One of the candidates was your party candidate. He came second. Then a democratic party candidate, one of the greatest Serbian writers of all time, Borislav Pekic. He came third. The candidate of the renewal movement came fourth. And at that time, my political adversaries dispersed an intrigue in the media that your party was actually pleased that I had won at the Rakovica elections, that it suited your purposes, and that it suited my settles of accounts with the pro-western opposition. Now, your -- it might have suited your party that I settled accounts with the pro-western opposition, but it certainly couldn't have suited your party to see my all-out election over your candidates. Quite simply, you didn't have a candidate who could have fought against me, had you nominated Borislav Jovic forward, I would have beat him too, with an overwhelming majority.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Seselj. You have answered that question very clearly, whether it could have been any kind of collusion, any collusion and collaboration in our relationships or any kind of cooperation between us or quite the contrary. You've answered that, that they excluded any possibility of collusion, and you said they did exclude any possibility of that kind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, please omit the comments. Just put your questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, after having quoted statements of yours for weeks, did Mr. Nice actually undermine his own thesis about joint criminal enterprise among us or did he perhaps strengthen it in that way?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I stopped that question, Mr. Milosevic, and you know the reason.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, the problem is that you cannot have the best of both worlds. On the one hand, that Mr. Seselj attacked me all the time, and that on the other hand, we were involved in a conspiracy of our own. And even resorting to the most derogatory terms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, utilise your time well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, Mr. Nice said that you had great access to the media and that you were in my favour. Those were his words. Tell me,

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Until you appeared as a candidate in the presidential elections in 1990, did you have any kind of wide access to the media?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Throughout 1990, I absolutely had no access to the media, not to a single TV station. In the election campaign, that was the first time when I appeared on state television. So what was under state control was totally unaccessible to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you first appeared on state television when, as a presidential candidate, you were allotted a certain amount of time, in accordance with the rules of the presidential elections, that every candidate should get a certain number [as interpreted] of time on air?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The state television could not avoid that. But only about ten days before that, I left prison. It was from prison that I put up my candidacy for president of the Republic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question is whether all presidential candidates had the right to equal time on television or whether you were privileged from that point of view.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: All candidates, and as far as I can remember, there were over 20 of them, had exactly one hour each on state television, whereas the order in which they appeared was decided by a lottery.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the election campaign, did the majority of the voters become familiar with your political programme and ideas?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In the daily press, they could read about various incidents that led to my arrests. That's what most of them could read about. In that year, I was arrested about 15 times, and three times I was sentenced to a term in prison.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Seselj, in response to Mr. Bonomy's question as to whether the indictment stating that all the participants in the joint criminal enterprise acted together, Mr. Nice says that he sticks to what the indictment said, that we did work together, not on our own. I don't know if I understood what he said. He can correct me if I misunderstood him. But after all, we can look at the transcript. So did we work in collusion or on our own?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is absolutely impossible. By definition, collusion means --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Wait a moment. Let's just look at something. In relation to this, because he answered Mr. Bonomy's question and he says that he still stands by what was stated in the indictment, that we acted in collusion. For example, if we look at paragraph 16 of the Kosovo indictment, when referring to the perpetrators, it says --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speaker please slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please slow down, Mr. Milosevic. A request from the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Nice reduced the indictment to acting in collusion. Could you please tell me whether, to the best of your knowledge, I and the remaining four persons mentioned, Milutinovic, Sainovic, Ojdanic and Stojakovic were acting in collusion, regardless of whether we're talking about legal activities or the commission of crimes. So how did we deal with the crisis in Kosovo and Metohija and how did we come to the situation there, or what were we doing? Were we doing something legal or were we acting in an underhanded way?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Collusion is impossible. Collusion is possible only when you're doing something illegal or semi-legal or something that is not morally proper or something like that. In this case, it is top state officials who had similar or identical tasks, and their high office made them cooperate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Do you have any direct knowledge about this, how each and every one of us, not to mention all the names again, all the persons who were mentioned by Mr. Nice, and I, how did every one of us come to the office from where we operated?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Through elections, direct or parliamentary elections. But everyone was elected through parliamentary elections.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. What were the rights and responsibilities that every one of us had? Did any one of us go beyond our authority? Did we use this authority and these powers in an impermissible way?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is not a shred of evidence of overstepping authority on the part of any one of the top state officials that you mentioned. There is not a single shred of evidence that anyone used his power in an illegal way. And there is no evidence of abuse of power. Everyone carried out their duties in accordance with the law and constitution. If they were not doing so, they would be committing a crime.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, if we acted within a constitutional framework and within the scope of the legal authority we had in terms of the office we held and the office is something that we got through democratic elections?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The authors of the indictment think that if Serbs are trying to defend their country and their people, then they commit a crime. And their organised defence of their country is a joint enterprise, a priori. That's how I see it. Serbs do not have the right to defend themselves, Serbs do not have the right to preserve their state, their people, they don't have the right to defend themselves from crime, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Seselj: I'm going to use a particular expression now. This expression used in the indictment "in concert with" and "in agreement with," do you think that they mean the same thing in the Serbian language?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It is quite different in the Serbian language. If you say "in concert with," or "in collusion with" and on the other hand, "in agreement with."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You probably know the official languages are English and French for authentic documents that are presented here. So in the English text it says: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues]... while in the French it says [Previous translation continues]... So in both languages that is what is said. In the Croatian and Bosnian indictment, it says: "In agreement with [B/C/S spoken]." Whereas in the Kosovo indictment it says [B/C/S spoken]. So the same word is used in English and in French in all the indictments. However, in the B/C/S version, the translation differs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: These are questions relating to interpretation and I don't understand how it is proper to put them to this witness. This is not the avenue for raising issues of that kind.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm asking the witness because when I'm putting a question to him, he has to understand what it's about and I have to understand it. He says that "in collusion with" and "in agreement with" cannot mean the same thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you're coming close to asking the witness about legal matters, which are properly the province of the Chamber. You're not allowed to put to the witness questions which the Chamber will ultimately have to answer itself.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, did you take part in any kind of reaching of agreement with me or other persons mentioned in that document, reaching any kind of agreement, particularly achieving anything that could be called joint criminal enterprise? It's a direct question and it pertains to you directly.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Throughout the war, Mr. Milosevic, we had daily consultations, practically every day. Perhaps we met at least three times a week. However, the subject of our talks, consultations, and agreements was never based on any intention to carry out any kind of criminal offence. That is what I state with full responsibility. All our agreements were aimed at strengthening efforts to defend the country. The economic power of the country, to defend the standard of living in a state of war, to provide water and other supplies, to ensure proper hygiene, et cetera. In a situation of war, it all functioned very well. It functioned better than it did in peacetime, which shows how highly organised we were. However, there was no criminal organisation, no organisation of a criminal nature. I am witness to the fact that several times you insisted on strict adherence of the law to protect civilians of any ethnic background and to prevent the commission of any crimes in a situation of war. All of those who were in contact with you during those days, during the war, can testify only to what I've said just now. There is no other possibility.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, since Mr. Nice is accusing me that I worked in collusion or in agreement with - so let us leave the vocabulary aside now - with some persons known and unknown, I believe that it is his duty to disclose the identity of these persons so that I would know how to respond. That should not be a problem for him, because he says persons known. As for persons unknown that he refers to, could you please explain this to me? How can I defend myself from accusations, not only I, but whoever acted together with me? But obviously Mr. Nice even doesn't know who it was that I acted with, so he's referring to persons unknown. I expect you to explain that. As for the persons known --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's a traditional method of drafting indictments to speak of persons known and unknown. It all depends on what arises in the evidence. We will look at the evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, Mr. Nice established here that the term "the Republic of Dubrovnik" was taken from the terminology that was used by the Serb authorities, and then he mentions the testimony of Pero Poljanic, the former mayor of Dubrovnik, and in his transcript there is no mention of that, that this was used by the Serb authorities. So did the Serb authorities ever use the term "the Republic of Dubrovnik"?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That term was only mentioned by the opposition, wishing to have a renewal of the Republic of Dubrovnik. Not a single state official of the Republic of Serbia ever stated those two words, "the Dubrovnik Republic," nowhere, at no time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When Mr. Poljanic testified, he said that at the head of this committee was Aco Apolonijo, a Croat, and for many years he was the public prosecutor in Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wish to correct you, Mr. Milosevic. I'm convinced that this Aco Apolonijo was a Catholic Serb, not a Croat, like all the old Dubrovnik families, they're all Catholic. But they're Serbs and they're proud of their Serbdom. Later on, being Croats was imposed on them by force.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When you refer to the opposition using the expression "Republic of Dubrovnik," do you mean yourselves, the Serb Radical Party?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Of course, Mr. Bonomy, I'm referring to myself and I've already said so. But now that you've asked me, I owe you an answer from last time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what it says here, what Mr. Nice said that: [In English] "Terminology used by the Serb authorities," [Interpretation] That's incorrect. It's not even what was stated by Pero Poljanic. Here, Mr. Seselj, you spoke of the difference between the JSO of the MUP of Serbia, that was called the Red Berets, that was established in 1996, and other units that were also called the Red Berets, one of which was established in Krajina in 1991. In order to verify what you said, I'm going to read out part of the transcript from the testimony of witness Dragan Vasiljkovic, Captain Dragan, when he testified here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, what is the point of this reading? What is the question that you want to put?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I want to ask Mr. Seselj this, his explanation, the quotation that Mr. Nice uses so often, the quotation of Mr. Simatovic from 1997. Does it coincide with the explanations given by Captain Dragan? I think that's very important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj is not in a position to answer that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Vasiljkovic, when he was explaining this here, said exactly the same thing as Mr. Seselj, the taking over of traditions and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's for the Chamber to make up its mind about those matters, Mr. Milosevic, not Mr. Seselj. Mr. Seselj is a witness. He's not the judge here.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that's precisely what I'm asking him. Does what he know coincide with the knowledge of that person, who was on the spot and who testified here?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No. That will not be allowed, and I've explained Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. why. Please ask another question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your cross-examination, Mr. Seselj, reference was made to Ustasha crimes. You spoke about Ustasha crimes from the World War II and the genocide against Serbs in the Independent State of Croatia. You were even asked by the Chamber to clarify certain terms. Let me quote to you from a statement by the Wiesenthal Center which calls the Ustasha camp of Jasenovac as follows: "Jasenovac was the largest camp in Croatia --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, what is the question that you wish to put?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it approximately the same as the explanation you gave when cross-examined by Mr. Nice, namely --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No. Mr. Milosevic, you're on very slippery ground here. You're not performing well the task of re-examination, the principal purpose of which is to seek to rehabilitate your witness in areas where you feel that his testimony may have been damaged, his credibility may have been damaged by cross-examination. It's not an opportunity to go over matters and to present your case again. It must relate to matters that arise out of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I think it follows directly from cross-examination and from the questions asked by Mr. Nice, as well as questions asked by you regarding the definition of "Ustasha," because in some of his questions, Mr. Nice identified Ustashas and Croats, whereas Mr. Seselj clearly distinguished between those two. So I want to ask him: Is that the notion reflected in the documents of the Wiesenthal Center that coincides with his own definition? So it reinforces what Mr. Seselj says and undermines the claims of Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I fail to see how we can be having this sort of quasi-expert -- at this stage. There must be a limit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I'm not allowing that. Please ask another question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. Robinson. Mr. Nice accused Mr. Seselj of instigating hatred. He said that the reactions of Serbs in Krajina in 1990 and 1991 were the results of his speeches and similar speeches by other politicians from Belgrade, rather than the real fear that prevailed there. So I hope you will not object to this question, since Mr. Seselj spoke about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will tell you what David Owen, who testified here, in his book "Balkan Odyssey" that was exhibited here, stated on page 34, paragraph 3. Can I read that or will you not allow me even that much?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: To what end? What is the question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, for the purpose -- I want to establish the exact cause of their reactions of Serbs in Krajina, Western Slavonia, Eastern Slavonia. What was the primary source of their fear? That's what I want to establish. Because Mr. Nice claims that Belgrade media, and this witness personally, unjustly spread fear and hatred, so that Serbs rose up in arms. That's the claim. That's the case of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, then simply ask him if he can say what was the cause of their fear.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Seselj, since they won't allow me to quote either Wiesenthal or Lord Owen, I will ask you the way Mr. Robinson suggests. What was the reason for such a situation?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reason always lay in the conduct of the Croatian leadership, that is, the Tudjman regime. Both political moves or military moves by the Serbs, they were all caused by Tudjman's behaviour. Even the crimes were never committed spontaneously by the Serb side. They were always a reaction to a previous Croatian crime. I have an article here from a newspaper that I can give to the Trial Chamber, which says that in October 1991, Croats killed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We have the answer to the question that Mr. Milosevic has raised. And Mr. Milosevic, Lord Owen's article and the statement that you refer to, the opportunity for you to refer to that will be in your closing address or in your brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, this fear that was created, fear of a repeat of genocide, was it based only on the memory of the Second World War or was there prior to that a return of Ustasha emigres, Sarinic and others, and did the Serbs associate the new Croatian regime with the previous Ustasha regime?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the manner in which you have put the question makes it a leading one, "Or was there prior to that a return of Ustasha emigres, Sarinic and others." You have to reformulate the question in a manner that is not leading.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let me put it in a non-leading way. Was it just a fear of a repeat of the events from the Second World War that caused the reaction of the Serb people at the time, or were there some tangible facts that caused this reaction?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: What happened in World War II constituted a terrible collective experience for the Serb people. But fear among them was caused by Tudjman's statement that the Independent State of Croatia had been an expression of historic aspirations of the Croat people. It is a fact that Ustasha emigres who had been abroad for dozens of years came back and came to the highest offices. There were also specific moves of the Croatian government directed at Serbs. I have another thing to say. Svetozar Livada, a famous Croatian sociologist and demographer compiled a study concerning the fate of Serbs in Croatia that was done for the Office of the Prosecutor. And I have here an article about that study, from which we can see how the Croatian government treated the Serbs. He established, by accurate, empirical methods, that 150.000 Serbs had been brutally expelled from Croatian towns where there had been no military action whatsoever. 25.000 Serb flats were seized and confiscated. That all happened in 1991, before the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To make it clear that it was not linked to the Second World War, that happened in 1990?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This study is being concealed by the Office of the Prosecutor, because it exposes their case as a lie. I just started to speak about the crime in the Pakrac valley --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I'm beginning to form the conclusion that you have exhausted all the useful questions that you have for re-examination. I don't see the direction at all of this re-examination. You seem to think that re-examination must be of a certain minimum length. I am not accustomed at all to re-examination lasting half an hour, 40 minutes, 50 minutes, and over. You have one or two points to re-examine on, five or ten minutes, and you finish. I have the duty to see that the time of the Court is used profitably, and I'm really beginning to doubt whether you have any more useful questions to put to this witness in re-examination. So I'm just going to get the view of my colleagues on this matter.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have very useful questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. You must put questions to the witness that are useful, that are helpful. Don't go over matters that the witness has already clarified. I've already told you in my -- re-examination is 10, 15 minutes, no more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I take it, Mr. Nice, the study referred to has been disclosed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm told it's been disclosed, then I suppose the answer is yes. But I'm not sure about it and I don't have the material available at the moment to check. But I will check. But in any event, this is not an opportunity or a time for the accused to be trying to get in material that would be expert in nature, if admissible at all. But I'll find out whether this one has been produced and come back to you on it. And of course if the accused wants to tell us that it was provided by us, and when, then that will help us in our research. But neither Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff nor I at the moment has any recollection of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We will try to establish when this was provided. Maybe Mr. Seselj knows.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The study by Svetozar Livada was done this year. It was so fresh that Mr. Nice should know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I appreciate fully what you are saying, and I would be very happy if I could finish my re-examination within ten minutes. But as far as I understand, re-examination must cover those points of cross-examination, selected points that are considered to be important, that I consider to be important, points on which I have to refute the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Not really. I mean, I think it depends on whether you think the witness needs to be rehabilitated. You are not obliged, and this may be the mistake, you should not feel obliged to respond to every point raised by the Prosecutor. In fact, if this were a trial with a jury, if this were a trial with a jury --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Far from it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- you would be giving the impression to the jury that the Prosecutor has done well in his cross-examination by spending so much time on re-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Well, juries are not professional, unlike you, so there is no such danger here, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a few more brief matters we have to cover. Mr. Nice quoted one of your texts addressed to pan-Islamists in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Mr. Nice claimed there were no pan-Islamists at the beginning of the crisis in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Do you know, maybe, was Alija Izetbegovic a pan-Islamist?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what he was in 1941?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a member of the terrorist organisation called the Young Muslims, and that's why he spent several years in prison. I don't know exactly how many.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know about the Handzar Division and the fact that it was rehabilitated, or rather, restored to existence before the war began?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have here the cover page of a Sarajevo magazine called Vox, 1991. As far as I know, the first conflicts arose in March 1992. That is true. However, later on, that unit was not called the Handzar Division any longer for fear of misunderstanding among the public. They called it the Green Berets. There was the official name for their unit. However, the people who made up or people who established that unit called it the Handzar Division amongst themselves.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we put this on the ELMO so that the witness can read the date and see briefly what this is about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Would the usher please put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you just read what it says on the cover page, on the front page of this Sarajevo magazine called Vox, read the date and describe what you see?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is all premised on the fact that I'm supposed to have claimed that there was no pan-Islamists at the beginning. Lots of things were said in the course of cross-examination, but I'd be grateful to be referred to the line and page of that observation. I don't recall with my recollection. Maybe there was some misunderstanding. Maybe the suggestion that I said such a thing is being used as a premise for getting in something that would otherwise be quite inadmissible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, are you in a position to refer us to the cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately, I'm not able to do that, no. I have not made a note of that. But I have made a note of this as, what shall I call it, a radical and flagrant untruth presented by Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As I say, I don't have any recollection of saying anything like that. It wouldn't have been my purpose to say any such thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Judge Kwon is ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We have located a question you asked,

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: "Could the Bosnian pan-Islamists fight a war against us Serbs?" That's a quotation from his book.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But Mr. Nice asked me whether it was possible that at that time already there were pan-Islamists in Bosnia, with respect to the fact that in the rest of the world they started to jeopardise it later on. I remember the substance of his question very well, and that was it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'll allow the question, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, we've just had a quotation from Mr. Robinson, whether they could have waged a war against the Serbs. Now, what date is that? When was it established?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the Sarajevo paper called Vox, which was printed and published in October 1991, that is to say, far before the real war in Bosnia-Herzegovina was unleashed. On the title page it says: "The Handzar Division is ready." And next to that it says: "The Fourth Reich is coming." And then in German, the word "willkommen" welcome. Now, this drawing shows a members of the Handzar Division, the SS marku Handzar Division, it's the SS Hitler division, marku, with a big knife stuck to his belt and underneath the cut-off heads of four Serbs. The one to the left is Radovan Karadzic's head. The one to the far right is my own severed head. And the two in the middle -- I can't recognise them just now. But anyway, that is it. And that was published in Sarajevo six months before the beginning of the civil war in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What has that got to do with pan-Islamists?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Hitler in World War II, for example, had ambitions of using the pan-Islamic factor and harnessing it to his own ends. And therefore he set up the SS Handzar Division in Bosnia for that purpose, and in Kosovo and Metohija the SS Skender Beg Division of Albanians. And he personally, the Jerusalem --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, hold on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The mufti of Jerusalem personally --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The two ideas are surely mutually inconsistent, the idea of being manipulated by Germans, on the one hand, and on the other hand, having the ambition of pan-Islam. They don't match each other.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it does go hand in hand, Mr. Bonomy, but you don't have the information. The mufti of Jerusalem personally, and his name was al-Husseini, during World War II came to Bosnia and dealt with business related to the establishment of the SS Handzar Division. And Hitler at that point in time considered that the Nazi factor could find its ally in the pan-Islamic factor. That is very highly consistent. But you don't have the patience to hear my detailed explanations about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, you've already had occasion to speak of your pedagogic tendencies, which have to be restrained here. Mr. Milosevic, I'm not satisfied with the way the re-examination is being conducted.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The expression "restrain" here has a rather negative connotation when translated into the Serb language. So I'd like to ask you not to use it perhaps. Perhaps it was the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, it doesn't have any unfortunate connotation in English. Mr. Milosevic, let me hear a question that is useful, that will advance your case, that is profitable, and that shows that you're using the Court's time well. Otherwise, I'm going to consider seriously terminating the re-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We won't continue that topic, Mr. Robinson, although I presented here the oath taken by the Young Muslims before the war and the Islamic declaration by Alija Izetbegovic which was republished in 1990, and I quoted some of the passages from the declaration. So it's quite clear what this is all about.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: For the record, I've finally been able to search LiveNote for pan-Islamists, and as far as I can see, there was never any question of mine framed in the way that the accused summarised it. All the references to pan-Islam came from this witness, one I think was a question from the Bench and otherwise it was him speaking. So it really is very unfortunate to see a great passage of evidence which is likely to be inflammatory, again when reported locally. The Chamber has to have this in mind. Put in now, I invite the Chamber frankly to bring this re-examination to a rapid close.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, your next question, and I'll be monitoring it very carefully. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Nice uses the term -- or rather, to show Serbian aggressivity, quoted a song that came from the football stadiums, and nobody could take it seriously, I don't think, at all. And as a protagonist of --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And -- I'm not going to make a comment myself.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, but I'm going to ask --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It is really trite of this -- silly of this accused to try and put in comments like that. The consequence of the sorts of songs that we've heard spoken of are a matter of evidence for others, not for him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I'm giving you one more chance, one more question. If it is not a useful question, then the Chamber will terminate the re-examination. We're wasting time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. Robinson. Does that mean that I can't ask him about those songs which Mr. Nice did ask about in the cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, there is nothing to be gained from that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, on many occasions, or a number of times, we identified here and didn't identify what Croats were and what Ustashas were. Do you remember the position by the founders of the Serbian Democratic Movement, or rather, Professor Raskovic, one of the founders, who said that we are not against the Croats but we are against the Ustashas? And that was his basic position in setting up the party.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I quoted that position of his I think on the first day of my testimony here. And he kept repeating that. He said that the Serbs and Serbian democratic movement had nothing against the Croats, that they are against the Ustashas, and he insisted upon that differentiation. And this did make a clear distinction between the two.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, Mr. Nice here introduced a number of documents which he had received from the government in Belgrade at his request that all documents be provided which mention or which are linked to 1995 and which mention Srebrenica, and I wanted you to take a look at those documents. I'd like you to look at them now, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could somebody help me here and provide copies for Mr. Seselj?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: If this is what Mr. Nice provided, I have this. I've saved it. It says here: "The command of the 1st Army report dated 1995," and they were given everything from 1995; is that right?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 13th of April, 1999. I have all those documents. I haven't thrown them away.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the interpreters please have a reference. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The interpreters are asking for a reference so that they can follow the evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This 03577655, ERN number, your number. And then there are more documents. There are a number of pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice can help us with the reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: While I'm doing that, just as a matter of practice, the witness said he had saved this document. I don't know if he means saved it on his desk, but of course when documents are provided to witnesses, they are for use in court, and the practice should not be that they take documents away with them, not least because the documents may be sensitive or protected. I don't know whether he meant that and I'm not seeking to sanction him. I'm checking on the practice. Because of course documents shouldn't be taken away from court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, I think, understands that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Exhibit 916, 916.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Exhibit 916. Thanks, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First, Mr. Robinson, nobody told me that I ought to return the documents. I threw the unimportant ones away after my testimony on a daily basis, and the ones that I consider to be more important, I kept them. I wasn't able to carry all the material in my bag. So what is Mr. Nice talking about when talking about sanctions? You know that I become afraid very easily and he's going to instil fear in me straight away. Well, I'm not going to return -- I can't return the documents unless the Trial Chamber instructs me to do so. Nobody can seize them from me unless the Trial Chamber orders me to return them. But it doesn't say that they are protected documents or confidential documents in any way. And had no mark of confidentiality on them except for the markings from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You must understand, and I think you understand, you are not to keep the documents. Leave the documents. The documents are in the custody of the Court. So the witness is not to take them away.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why didn't you tell me that on day one, Mr. Robinson? Nobody told me that, ever. I took the documents away. I threw some away. I made a selection. And you're telling me this now, when everything is over. I really don't understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I regret that, Mr. Seselj. You're so learned, I thought you would have known that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There's a problem that the witness incidentally publishes large numbers of court documents on his website. Maybe a specific order ought to be made that he is to do nothing further with and to return existing copies he has of exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I can't for the life of me understand why any witness would think he had any right to take anything he was given in court out of court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Let us -- Mr. Seselj, do you have documents that you have taken out of court? If you have such documents, you must return them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do have some documents which I took with me and carried around with me from the time that Mr. Nice provided me with them. They are the set of documents with respect to the request made to the authorities in Belgrade for assistance, request for assistance, to be provided with the documents, and what the authorities from Belgrade sent. And that's all I have with me. Other material which are photocopies of my books, I generally threw away, although I like one of the photographs a lot and kept that one. But this is what might be stamped "confidential," but then that should be stated and said. I don't know how long my testimony -- I didn't know how long my testimony would last in respect to each of these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You have heard what I have said. If you have taken court documents, you must return them. Let us proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, we're just going to go through this before we move on to the documents. Or rather, let me ask you this: To the best of your knowledge about the situation of our country at the present point in time and the authorities there, can we reasonably assume that everything requested by that opposite side there --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, this is provocatively leading and inappropriate. We are coming to the break, and you will not be allowed to re-examine beyond the break. That's in two minutes, two or three minutes. You're clearly running out of steam.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I have a lot more material, Mr. Robinson, and I have very concrete, specific questions to ask the witness, which Mr. Nice omitted to ask him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, you can see these documents. Here we have a report by the command of the 1st Army, which relates to the 13th of April, 1995.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we see here the state in the border belt, that is, the heading? Can you see that heading? And then we go the border with Romania, the situation on the former -- it says territory, border with Romania, border with Hungary, border with Serbian Krajina, under D, the border with the Republic of Croatia, and E, border with Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, is there any difference in the treatment of all these borders from the aspects of the military authorities?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The treatment of all these borders from the aspects of the military authorities is identical. They are treated in the same way. The borders towards Republika Srpska as indeed the borders towards Romania, Hungary, and other countries.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what does it say in the last paragraph under E, borders towards Republika Srpska, for example? Read that out to us.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The forces of the Army of Republika Srpska --"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Not that. I meant the last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see, the last paragraph. "Activities of the -- intensive activities of the UN alpha monitoring mission were focussed on covering the border crossing with Republika Srpska, monitoring of the Drina River, and the way the SRJ decision, Federal Republic of Yugoslavia decision on closing the border with Republika Srpska were being introduced."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not going to dwell on this any longer, this particular document. So this is the time when there was a monitoring mission there. Please look at the next document now of the command of the 1st Army, dated the 7th of June, 1995.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We have here in paragraph 1 a statement to the effect that two tank shells fell in the area of Mali Zvornik. So that's right on the border. And nothing else of any particular significance. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The most interesting document that Mr. Nice provided here is the document of the command of the 2nd Army, dated the 17th of July, 1995. That is the time when what happened in Srebrenica had already happened.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Gentlemen, the 2nd Army includes the south-western part of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, doesn't have a border towards Romania or Croatia. It has a border towards Albania and Republika Srpska. So you have here the situation in the border area towards Albania and Republika Srpska. So 1.1. The Republic of Albania. It only indicates some smuggling or whatever else is established, so we're going to skip that. And what is the section about Republika Srpska say?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Bozidar Babic, as Commander of the 2nd Army, tells the General Staff the following: In the former territory of Republika Srpska, in the area of Gorazde, in the second half of May, the situation was getting worse, especially after the withdrawal of UNPROFOR members from the observation posts, which Muslim forces used to take over the facilities south-east from Gorazde, the village of Gornje Kolijevke, the village of Pagani, Samari, feature 586, elevation .586, where they are still located. In the second half of June, around the Muslim enclaves in Eastern Bosnia, on the foreign territory combat operations were carried out every day. On the 26th of May, 1995, the Muslims from the Zepa enclave, with five to ten soldiers, formed a border post in the area of Zibine, elevation 8939, and Trnovac, elevation 989 on the foreign territory of the border post Jagostica, and from these observation posts they were observing our territory every day."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this is the army whose area of responsibility includes the entire border area on the banks of the Drina River, to the west are the enclaves of Zepa and Srebrenica. Mr. Seselj, what did our military organs learn about the situation in the enclaves and what is contained in these documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The witness, I think, told us about his movements in and out of gaol in 1995. He's asked extensively for documents upon which he had relied to give you the generalised and exculpatory account of Srebrenica and said that these documents were, so far as he could see, documents he had never seen before. So where are we going with this? Is this re-examination on the documents or is this some kind of repeat examination on what he's heard by way of, so he tell us, generalised hearsay for events in Srebrenica? What value can it conceivably be?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is only examination on the documents that Mr. Nice tendered here. So the most authentic document, the document of the command of the 2nd Army, in whose area of responsibility is the border area towards Republika Srpska. And on the other side, are those enclaves. So this document shows what our army knew at that time about those events. And it can be seen that they knew nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But that is in the document. We'll see that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the document, they write about what they know. The commander of the army informs the General Staff about everything they know from the border area facing Romania, Bulgaria, Albania and so on. So obviously, they did not know about what was going on in Srebrenica except for what is referred to here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That seems to be the comment, and the accused is of course missing the point, either intentionally or accidentally, not being a qualified lawyer as advocate, that these documents were presented to show the limit of provision by the authorities in respect of the request for documents relating to the Srebrenica period, and for the purpose of seeing if they were some of the documents upon which this witness had relied. Having had his answers on that second point, it's doubtful whether he can serve any purpose by going through these documents in the way --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I agree. We'll not hear it. It's 25 minutes to 11.00. Mr. Milosevic, I'm going to consult with my colleagues in the break about your re-examination. How many more questions do you have?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I have about ten or so questions left, and I consider them to be most important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we'll sit for another five minutes and then that will be the end of the re-examination. With the indulgence of the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't know. I can't manage to finish within five minutes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I'll not allow you more than five minutes, so please start.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please look at the next document, Mr. Seselj. That is a report on the work of the monitoring mission, the command of the Uzice Corps.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What does it say here? From the conflict in Eastern Bosnia broke out in the enclaves of Zepa and Srebrenica, Bajina Basta considerably reduced its activity, et cetera, et cetera, and then does it not explain --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: This is not useful. We have the document here. We can read it. It's not the purpose of re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, what about the next document of the information department of the General Staff that gives information about the current military political and security situation? Does it refer to Zepa and Srebrenica at all or the position of the FRY in relation to that?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the third paragraph. Even an assessment is provided, according to which the attacks and takeover of Srebrenica and Zepa were measured only in relation to military results, but they had great political damage --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Great political damage, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the next page, the third paragraph from the bottom, it says something about the position of how right the position of the FRY was to end the war and accept peace initiatives and plans as totally justified and correct, taking into account the interests of all the sides that are involved in the conflict. Next?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Therefore, it is quite understandable that all attempts to involve Yugoslavia in the conflict lead to a catastrophe of the Serbian people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on the last page?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the interpreters please be given time to find it.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is information signed by Slavko Krivosija.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next one, again of the command of the 2nd Army. The situation towards the Republic of Albania and then towards Republika Srpska. On the 16th of October, 1995. What does it say towards the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: "In the border area --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, this is pointless. The re-examination --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- is concluded. We adjourn now for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, Mr. Robinson, I have to put Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. a question to Mr. Seselj in relation to the document provided by Mr. Nice and that has to do with his statement. That is a very important question, a very important one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Why didn't you put it before?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, because I'm taking a particular order in which I worked, Mr. Robinson. I don't understand why you're limiting me in this way. Mr. Nice spent far more time here quoting paragraph 25 from this document of the Serb Radical Party, in relation to Albanian separatists and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: One last question. One last question and then we adjourn.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, please, take Exhibit 911.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: What's that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is your speech in the parliament, in the Assembly, on the 7th of April, 1992. And Mr. Nice's assertion that that was the cause for expelling Croats. And you explained that not a single Croat was expelled from Serbia, which is correct, but he said that that was the policy that prevailed at that time in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
