utterances.text: I don't have the speech in front of me now, but I remember very well that the president of the National Assembly reacted to it, Aleksandar Bakocevic, and that he disassociated himself from the substance of that speech.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll give you a copy of the speech. Your speech first and then what the president of the National Assembly said. And while the usher is taking this to you: Is it customary for the president of the National Assembly to make comments on speeches made by MPs?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This point was made in the course of the cross-examination. This is where the speaker reprimands or tries to reprimand the witness. And we've got the point already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Bonomy. I'm terminating the re-examination now, Mr. Milosevic. We'll adjourn now for 20 minutes and then we'll have your next witness. Thank you for coming to give evidence, Mr. Seselj. The evidence is concluded and you may leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: A couple of matters arising from the testimony of the last witness. There was reference to a report served on the accused by the Office of the Prosecutor. We've investigated that, and the name is just one syllable different, not that we would have, I suggest we would have remembered the name even if it had been correctly spelled. It's Svetozar Livada and a statement from that person was taken in fact not by the Milosevic case team or indeed the Seselj case team. I think by another case team, but under the usual cautious steps we take to deal with material that may be Rule 68 in part or whole, it was served on the accused in May of this year. The second point arising from the evidence of this witness: The Chamber asked me last week a question about any duties on Serbia to investigate Srebrenica, and I omitted one point that the Chamber might have wanted to have in mind, and that is that as from the 1993 resolution of the United Nations, which is in evidence, and I'll find the number of it, if necessary, there was a duty on all the parties, and particularly the FRY, to have regard to what was happening or possibly going to happen in Srebrenica. And then the Chamber will probably remember that Jovanovic was asked about and gave evidence about letters that he sent to a number when at the United Nations, in one of which he sought to blame the Bosnians themselves for what had befallen them, a letter I think which he perhaps subsequently disowned or abandoned in part or whole. And in the course of that evidence - again, we can find the detail, if necessary - the Chamber may recall that he explained how he had relied upon information coming from the RS to justify the letters that he sent. So that's the beginning and end stages of another possible process of duty for -- process whereby duty fell on the Serbs to investigate Srebrenica. Your Honours, before Delic is recalled for re-examination, General Delic, two things about him. First, the Chamber will know from filings that there are applications in respect of documents that he might be able to assist with. Of course, they aren't yet here, if any are going to be ordered. And that's simply a problem that --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Simply a problem that may mean that the Chamber would want to be cautious about saying that he's finished with for good, because he may be the subject of an application for recall. And more specifically worrying or concerning is this: The Chamber will recall that a very large quantity of the material he has sought to produce in evidence was material produced for something called the VJ Commission. And the Chamber will remember, because this is in evidence, that was a body that was abolished almost immediately on the ascension to office of minister of defence by Boris Tadic in the spring of 1993, with comments on the nature of and it may be integrity of that particular body. The Chamber may recall that we were going to make efforts to have before you for the re-examination of this witness the documents held by the authorities into that -- relating to that VJ Commission, dealing both with its creation, and more particularly, with the reason for its ending in the way that it was ended, by then Minister of Defence Tadic. Now, the history is extremely unfortunate. A request, an urgent request, was made on the 6th of July by the Prosecutor herself to the relevant minister, and an earlier response was received to the effect that the documents concerned dealing with that commission were being pulled out and produced on the 7th of July. They were the subject of repeated requests for processing, with various explanations, if explanations is the right word, being given for how documents produced on the 7th of July, limited in number, were not being produced to this Court for its use with a witness who was coming back. Eventually, last week, the position was made clear that if these documents weren't available, why, then, of course it might not be possible to conclude with the witness's evidence, i.e., to put it another way, delaying the production of the documents until after he had given his evidence might not, in a sense, dispose of the matter. Finally, and in response to the repeated pressure that's being put on the authorities by us through our local office and otherwise, we were told the documents were provided yesterday afternoon, and they are in the process of being faxed to this Court now. So two and a half months has passed since an urgent request was made and apparently positively responded to by the authorities. And we will have the documents to peruse sometime this morning or this afternoon or tomorrow. We don't know what, if anything, they will provide by way of potentially useful material for the Chamber or what they might provide us if we were minded to seek leave to ask further questions of the witness. It is extremely unfortunate. The Chamber will recall that the VJ Commission documents, the documents the production of which I challenged -- the production of exhibits of which I challenge on the ground on the grounds that they were not contemporaneous, they may of course have been distributed for oblique purposes, the documents going to show the composition of the VJ Commission, instituted as I believe it was by Pavlovic, with other members of the high authorities, either before this Court in other trials or implicated in various ways, being just one of its characteristics. So Your Honours, I'm afraid I would violate the Chamber to be alert to the possibility that although this witness may give some evidence in re-examination today, it may be the case that I will be asking for him to be brought back on a subsequent occasion to deal with VJ Commission documents and/or with other documents that may be produced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: If the Chamber agrees.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Of course if the Chamber agrees. But, Your Honour, these are serious matters. In relation to the application for documents, the Chamber knows the Prosecution's position on how cooperation has or more particularly not taken effect. It was perfectly apparently that Delic had access one way or another to documents on a far more generous basis than that which is said to be possible in filings with this Chamber. So that's one point. And these are documents, if they are now available and can be produced, that may be central to various of the issues of his evidence. And as to the commission documents themselves, they go absolutely to the issue, challenged from the beginning by the Prosecution of whether his proposed exhibits should be exhibited at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll bring you up to date with position on commission documents as they come and as we are able to scan them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness be brought in. Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the transcript, I want to object very strongly to your decision to stop the re-examination of witness Vojislav Seselj. It's not the first time you do it. You did the same thing with General Obrad Stevanovic, and now you've done the same thing with Vojislav Seselj. I had an entire series of questions left for him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And I want to make it absolutely clear: I will do it again. I will do it in relation to this witness if you do not use the time of the Court profitably. I'm very upset with you. So if you re-examine in that same manner, your re-examination is going to be terminated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Delic, you remain subject to the declaration that you made. Mr. Milosevic, you may -- Mr. Delic is not hearing the translation. Yes. I was saying that you remain subject to the declaration that you made. And Mr. Milosevic, you may begin the re-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I begin my re-examination, Mr. Robinson, regarding the comments made by Mr. Nice prior to this concerning documents received by the authorities in Belgrade, I wish to have an explanation as to whether I have received those documents as well, and will they be the subject of some additional examination by Mr. Nice during this particular stay of the witness in The Hague, or will he be asking to recall him?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The position is that Mr. Nice will make his mind up as to whether he wishes to apply to the Chamber for further cross-examination of the witness. The Chamber will then decide that issue. If the Chamber grants such an application, then, naturally, you would be able to re-examine on that, if re-examination is necessary, and you will then be entitled to see all the documents used in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Re-examined by Mr. Milosevic: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then to begin with, I wish to draw your attention to the fact that on the 15th of September, that is, at the end of last week, I received a communication from Mr. Nice. It contains, as it says here, witness information provided by Paddy Ashdown on the 24th of August this year. I don't know if the witness is in possession of this information or not. I see him shaking his head, meaning no. It has to do, though, with the part of the testimony of General Delic where he denied that Paddy Ashdown could have physically been able to see the things he claimed to have seen from the place where he was at the time. Since the witness hasn't seen this information --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, do you want to have that document passed to the witness in order to ask a question, or do you want to have it put on the ELMO? What's your position?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I suppose that the document is only in English. If there is a Serbian version, then I would like it passed to the witness. If it hasn't been translated, then perhaps it should be put on the ELMO so that the witness can have read to him the important parts, skipping all the points regarding procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Ms. Dicklich personally provided the accused with a version in B/C/S this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You heard that, Mr. Milosevic. You were provided with a B/C/S version by Ms. Dicklich personally. Am I to thank her on your behalf?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can do that. But I didn't review it in detail, because the front page is the same, and I didn't know that what she gave me was a translation. But obviously we do have a translation now. Could the witness have this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You don't have a copy, do you? All right. Re-examined by Mr. Milosevic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's the statement of Mr. Ashdown. General, could you start reading from the fourth paragraph, because the first three paragraphs are not so important to the questions that I'm going to ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If the B/C/S version could be handed over to the witness and put the English version on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Here's the English version. Now I'm left without either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's an unusual position for you, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, would you kindly read from the Serbian text the last three paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "In relation to my testimony concerning my observations on Tuesday, 23rd June 1998, from a monitoring point above Gegaj, Kosovo, the grid reference from which these observations were made was approximately 34T DM359982. From this position, I could see the area south of Junik, including the villages of Molic, Brovina and Ponosevac. I could see two roads from here, the road along which Molic, Brovina and Ponosevac are located and a road to the east on which the villages of Novokaz, Berjah and Stubla are located. I saw tanks situated along the latter road shelling the village on the former road. In relation to my testimony concerning my observations on 27 September 1998, from a position close to Studencane, Kosovo, the grid reference from which these observations were made was approximately 34T DM804898. From this position I could see what I described as the Dolje Blace feature. This feature runs between grid references 34T DM915954 and 34T DM888968. In relation to my testimony concerning my observations from a position close to the village of Pecani, Kosovo, on 28 September 1998, I estimate the grid reference from which these observations were made to be 34T DM863920. From this position, I testified that I could see the villages of Budakovo which is at grid reference 34T DM945891, Macitevo, Gornji Krusico which is at grid reference 34T DM944902, and Krusico."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before I start questioning you, General: In the first paragraph, it says the village of Gegaj, Kosovo. Is this village in Kosovo or in Albania?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's in Albania, of course. I have to say one more thing at the outset. In order to be able to answer any question regarding this, I need some time, because grid references indicated here belonged to a totally different system of coordinates, which means I need maps in order to find these elevations on the ground. I could certainly not speak about it today.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, I received from my associates a review of visibility from various points around Gegaj village on the Orahovac-Suva Reka axis. It was prepared from the experts from the Military Geographic Institute. Could you explain that, because Mr. Nice insisted on this point.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. But I would like --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm not sure where we're being done preparatory to the witness coming to be able to be in a position to give a review of documents that apparently have just fallen into possession of the accused. I invite the Chamber to clarify matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think it relates to the issue as to whether Mr. Ashdown was in a position to see what he said he saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. But it's the reference to a whole new series of documents coming from associates, prepared by experts. I can't see the way this can come in in re-examination, and I'm a little concerned about the fact that the witness appears to be already in a position to deal with them. That I don't understand, but maybe I'm missing the point. Of course in re-examination, there's no way he can know about these things in advance.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can certainly speak about anything that has to do with military topography. I can also comment on this document related to Lord Ashdown. But you have to understand that he Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. provided certain coordinates here. I don't have maps here. I don't have the equipment to measure coordinates, and I cannot determine where these points are. That's the only problem. Otherwise, it's not a problem to calculate. It's pure mathematics. Once I make the calculation, I would be able to see those points on the map and express my view as to what Mr. Ashdown was able to see or not. But I need time to transfer these grid references to our system of coordinates, and I need maps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, it's not clear to me what the question that you're seeking to put relates to. Is it to Paddy Ashdown's statement, the portion of his statement which was put on the ELMO, or is it in relation to a new set of documents that you are seeking to introduce, documents that you received from your associates?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I wish to remind you that we have had testimony by Paddy Ashdown concerning what he was able to see from various observation points. The witness, in his turn, had explained that Mr. Ashdown could not have seen those things from those points. Then we received the additional explanation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We are familiar with the history. But what is it that you're seeking to do? Are you now seeking to put in documents which you said you received from certain experts?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Those are not new documents. They are just more precise, better documents. And in view of the shortness of time and the fact that Mr. Nice wanted the witness to find something on the map and mark the map, and that it was a very improvised exercise, I had three different pictures of various axes around Junik and the cross-section of the relief on that axis. All that was derived from the relief, from the computer. It was done properly and in a way that shows exactly where these points are. So I want Mr. Delic to look at these maps when we place them on the ELMO, and they were prepared by the military institute. And Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, has Mr. Delic already seen these documents?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These documents?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, the documents which you are now seeking to put.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, he hasn't. I have no capacity to contact Mr. Delic. This is something that my associates obtained from an expert institute. These are 3-D pictures of all these axes indicated in the testimony of Mr. Ashdown, and the additional statements introduced by Mr. Nice. So this is a very precise calculation. Instead of the improvisation we had last time, we have 3-D computer designed picture now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: My submission, this material shouldn't go forward at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Because it's expert material that's being produced through a witness in re-examination. How can that help? Let me explain -- let me remind the Chamber of what the position is. Lord Ashdown gave evidence of what he could see and spoke of his approximate position. He wasn't challenged then on visibility issues at all. Nothing was put to him to suggest that his evidence, which of course had been disclosed in advance in the statements in the usual form, was disprovable on these particular grounds. It may have been challenged in general grounds, but I don't think it was challenged on the grounds of you couldn't see what you said you could see from there. It doesn't matter if it was challenged, because that's the way the evidence left. This witness came, without advance notice to us, of course, and said, Well, from this approximate position you can't see this and you can't see that. That was then dealt with by our obtaining reactions from Lord Ashdown, in as much detail as we could in the circumstances, through maps, which the witness was invited to mark and which Lord Ashdown and others marked and prepared, for the purposes of cross-examination. The issue was clearly one that might rumble on, and so Lord Ashdown was invited to and did provide a further statement which was served on the accused. There's another statement forthcoming when it's ready - it hasn't yet been finally prepared - which contains -- which has attached to it a video showing what can be seen from the particular grid reference points to which Lord Ashdown refers. And of course, it will be my application that this material can go in in re-examination. Now, that's -- in rebuttal, I'm so sorry. In rebuttal. So that's the present and prospective evidential position in accordance with the normal rules of court and the normal order of calling evidence. For the accused to be able to put through this witness in re-examination what is apparently expert material of a kind that has not been the subject of any advance notice that an expert report is to be forthcoming and is not to be supported by the witnesses themselves seems to me to be valueless. I can't cross-examine on it. I can do nothing about it. It's the accused through this witness who has raised this issue by taking by surprise the Prosecution with the assertion that these things simply couldn't be visible from that vantage point, without serving expert evidence in advance. We've reacted to it in various ways but to the limit of our ability and we're now in a position to serve rebuttal evidence. If this accused wishes to add to the evidence on this topic by experts, he should call the experts, and then I can deal with it. I have the expert report in advance, I can see what it shows by way of photographs, videos, grid references, I can make my inquiries and either accept or challenge the answers. Coming in through re-examination, I can do nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can I just raise a matter? The Court will recollect the cross-examination in which sketches and topographical drawings were put in by the Prosecutor to the witness, and he was told to deal with them. And he responded accordingly, saying that these landmarks identified by Lord Ashdown could not be seen. So in a sense, the Prosecution have caused this issue to be raised in the trial by the production of documents by them which the Defence is seeking to deal with, and said at the time that they would deal with, by obtaining material from a geographical institute, giving the contours of the land. And that was the suggestion that came from the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What about the procedural point that Mr. Nice makes in relation to notification for expert evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The witness is in fact an expert. He's told us that there's probably none better at looking at maps than him, and I think he's taken us through enough maps in the course of his testimony for that foundation to be justified. And he is seeking to deal, through his own evidence, which has been challenged by the Prosecution, of matters that they indeed raised in cross-examination, which doesn't seem to be objectionable. It's probative and relevant. Like many witnesses, he has an expertise in the subject about which he is talking. He's a witness of fact, has been to the area, and happens to have a particular skill which he says justifies his conclusions and the evidence that he has given to the Trial Chamber. It seems unduly onerous to have to go to someone once removed from him to start the process and argument all over again when he is plainly the party who has been challenged by the Prosecution over his evidence and can deal with it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I be allowed to add something here? Please bear in mind the fact that General Delic testified about the events in the area of his responsibility, which is very well known to him, and that these three-dimensional images which I wish to offer relate to parts of the area of responsibility that he was in control of, which he knows well about and which were mentioned by Paddy Ashdown. And the witness explained that Paddy Ashdown could not have seen those places from the points that he was standing at. So we had the insinuations made by Mr. Nice when he asked the witness to draw in pencil where and what could be seen. We now have a three-dimensional image taken off the computer of the terrain that the witness testified about and challenged Paddy Ashdown's testimony. So I do not see why we need an improvisation which, at the request of Mr. Nice, the witness prepared and drew, without looking at a professional, three-dimensional photograph of the lie of the land at each of these individual localities that we're talking about. So how can that do any harm? Something that is more precise be less important from something that is less precise?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, at first sight, this seems a very pertinent piece of evidence to bring. But it seems to me this isn't the way to do it. The way to do it is to bring the person who did this. Because we've got a dispute between two witnesses. And if you bring a third person in to look at it from a particular point of view, that would be very helpful to the Trial Chamber. But simply to ask this witness about something he had no hand in doing seems to me pretty pointless, and even beyond that, unfair, if it's then not open to the Prosecution to challenge it, because of the way in which it's been presented.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The feature was --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Judge Kwon is speaking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I remember some picture of topographs which was put to the witness, was prepared by an expert on the part of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There were a series of documents that were produced.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There were a series of documents that were produced. First of all, he was asked to mark a map. He found the first map unacceptable. He was given a range of maps. He eventually marked another map. That, I think, if my recollection is correct, was then made available to Lord Ashdown, and he prepared one chart in hand, looking at the maps himself, and a further chart was prepared by Phil Coo, the military expert who had given evidence on behalf of the Prosecution, again to show lines of sight from estimated positions identified by Lord Ashdown. I think that's as far as it went. And so that's as far as it goes in the production of expert material. But this, of course, was in cross-examination, which is different from re-examination. And I'm plainly entitled, when an issue is raised like this, to put what would be my case at the next stage, if it's granted, of the calling of evidence. That was not accepted by the witness, and so we've moved on to gather further expert evidence. And it seems to me, with great respect, that what's being planned is simply unhelpful and not going to take us anywhere further unless dealt with properly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, may I be allowed to say something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a moment, Mr. Delic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, at this stage, we'll take a procedural approach to the issue. The witness has said he's not in a position to deal with Mr. Ashdown's statement. So we'll wait until tomorrow, let him have this evening to look at Paddy Ashdown's statement, and then tomorrow we'll deal with the question of the admissibility of the documents that you are seeking to put in.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, can I ask you to agree to allow me to give the witness this three-dimensional image, because he has Paddy Ashdown's statement, that it be accompanied with this three-dimensional image. They are geographical maps. There's nothing else there, no other explanations except the maps themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is there any reason why that shouldn't be done, Mr. Nice?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. That may be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Presumably, I'll get a copy as well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just to draw your attention to the fact that apart from the images, there is a table of visibility and audibility, the topographical data, military topographical data of the General Staff of 72 to 79. So the relevant document is that, apart from the photographs, and the photographs are in colour. Here you have them. And I should like to ask my associates to provide a set of those images to Mr. Nice and to you yourselves in the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's very gracious of you, Mr. Milosevic. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But to be absolutely fair to the witness of Mr. Nice's, Mr. Ashdown, I would like this to be placed on the ELMO as well. It is Birmingham Post, September the 2nd, 2005, and a Friday. That's the date. An article appearing in the Birmingham Post, mentioning the fact that Paddy Ashdown was an agent of MI 6. So perhaps Mr. Ashdown --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is this, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's an article from your own newspapers, an article from your newspaper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is this relevant to?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's relevant to the fact that Paddy Ashdown, quite obviously, supported the terrorists in Kosovo and Metohija, as indeed today he is supporting all those events in Bosnia-Herzegovina which are to the detriment of the Serb people in Republika Srpska, and is creating them, not only supporting them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: While it might not be obvious, I have exhibited a great deal of restraint this morning. I would have brought the re-examination of the last witness to an end earlier than it was brought to an end. And it seems to me this is another obviously blatant attempt to abuse re-examination. And I will be for bringing this one to an end also if the abuse continues.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm grateful for Your Honour's observations. I remind the Chamber that these proceedings are serving oblique purposes by their publication elsewhere. But those are purposes that may have dangerous and serious consequences, and that must be borne in mind, in our respectful submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, proceed to another question. Bear in mind my observations earlier about terminating re-examination, as well as the remarks just made by Judge Bonomy.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I would have to bear in mind what Mr. Nice said too, so I can respond to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, when you testified about air support of NATO planes to KLA terrorists, which were active on the ground, Mr. Robinson was particularly interested in this collaboration between the KLA and NATO. Namely, on page 41978 of the transcript, you will be able to find the following words by Mr. -- uttered by Mr. Robinson. So it is 41978, the transcript page. "[In English] It really is a question that has fundamental legal implications for the case, because if that is so, the nature of the conflict is changed. You have a group of states whom you say are acting with terrorist forces, and in my view, if you are responding to that attack, that implicates Article 51 of the United Nations Charter, and that's why -- that's the importance of that question." [Interpretation] My question to you, General, is this: With the state organs of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, including the army of Yugoslavia, the Ministry of the Interior, as well as with the population of our country, was there the general view that our army and police were acting in self-defence? Was that the general view that was held by these --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you are moving in the same direction as you were this morning. You very well know you cannot ask the witness that kind of question. That's a legal issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There are two possibilities here: Either you're incapable of conducting this re-examination or you're deliberately abusing the privilege. The first one could be resolved by inviting Mr. Kay to deal with it, and then we might get some sensible questions. And the second one can only be resolved by bringing it to an end.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, very well. I can reformulate the question. The General is testifying --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's pointless to rephrase a question that has been put in those terms. The whole purpose has been destroyed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, then. Mr. Bonomy, would this be a suitable question, if I say -- if I ask whether the state organs, including the army and the Ministry of the Interior and the population, held the general view that there was an aggression being exerted against the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's equally impermissible, equally impermissible.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, all right, then. Are you going to tell me this is impermissible too, for me to ask the witness whether the word "aggression" was used in official and unofficial terminology and to what extent, during the aggression exerted by NATO against Yugoslavia? Is that impermissible too? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is the point of that question? What's the point of it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the point of it is in the fact that in what you describe very well, Mr. Robinson, yourself, that it was a question of a joint effort against Yugoslavia -- an attack against Yugoslavia by the KLA bands in the territory and by NATO itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The factual basis for that kind of submission from you on self-defence has already been laid through this witness and others. You can't get anything more from this witness. He can't tell you whether you're acting in self-defence. That's a legal issue. That's a matter for us. It's a matter for you to make submissions on in your address and in the legal brief that you will present. This witness can't help you on that issue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Can the witness help, then, with regard to the following fact: Since he was commander of the units in the area of responsibility in the part of the territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia facing Albania, can he testify to military intervention coming from Albania, as well as -- intervention that was carried out by NATO and Albania? Can he answer that question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. But you should be more specific.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you saying that that's something that he hasn't already given evidence about?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He has given evidence about many concrete events, many concrete events that corroborate that. I'm asking him about his knowledge in general, about the foreign factors acting in conjunction, that is to say, the Republic of Albania and NATO troops on its territory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In my opinion, that's not appropriate re-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bonomy, in Article 3(G), there is the following definition of "aggression": "[In English] Armed bands, groups, irregulars or mercenaries which carry out act of armed force against another state of such gravity as to amount to the acts listed above or a substantial involvement therein." [Interpretation] So this is a very important question that I am asking General Delic about, and I add the following: From when was this form of aggression applied against the FRY?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm afraid I'm lost, really. I don't know what he's talking about. I don't know how he says it's relevant. And I don't know where the premise is that there was aggression applied against the FRY. Very mysterious to me. It seems to be irrelevant and should be eliminated from the re-examination. The accused should be invited to move on or stop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, there is merit in that submission. We have evidence on this issue already. These are matters that you have already raised. And it's not appropriate for re-examination. So move on to another issue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, Mr. Nice showed you a letter of General Perisic sent to me. I'm not going to qualify it in terms of whether it's true or not, but what is referred to are certain abuses of the army, illegal command, imposing martial law, et cetera. Could you please explain the rules of service of the army of Yugoslavia that you mentioned in response to these assertions made by Mr. Nice. If you do not remember exactly what this was about, I can jog your memory. If you do remember, you can say that you remember and you can explain.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I remember. Mr. Nice showed me this letter. And the essence of this letter was that Mr. Perisic believes that the units of the Army of Yugoslavia could not have been used in peacetime without imposing martial law in order to resolve the very difficult situation in the area of Kosovo and Metohija. Even then I referred to the rules of service.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please pause for a moment. Could you explain, General, what the rules of service are.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is one of the basic documents of the army, based on the constitution, on the law on the Army of Yugoslavia, which regulated the entire life and work of the army and how the army would act in different situations. That would be the briefest possible explanation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do we know the exhibit number of the rules of service?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is this in evidence, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope it is, but I'll have to check. I cannot say now off the top of my head. I have not brought in that huge bundle of documents that he had in front of him while testifying, so I'll check during the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you should know this. This is something that you are putting to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I've put before the witness are the allegations made by Mr. Perisic, and I asked him to comment upon that and to assess how truthful those allegations are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But I asked you whether the document was in evidence, and you are not in a position to say.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that it has been admitted into evidence, Mr. Robinson, but as I've said, I'm going to check. I cannot be certain of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Rules of service for security organs of the armed forces of the former Yugoslavia came in through the witness Mustafa Candic, Exhibit 350, tab 2, but it's security organs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Kay. What is the specific question you're putting to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My specific question to the witness is whether it was possible to use the units of the army without imposing martial law, in cases of terrorism or securing communications, that is to say, the functioning of normal life on the ground. Because that was the point, that martial law would have to be imposed so that anyone could use the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, I'll allow the witness to answer that, if he can.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the rules of service, I know that at the request of the OTP, I got my own rules of service out and sent them to the commission for cooperation. So it should be here. When we talked about this, Mr. Nice referred to the exact article in the rules of service pertaining to this question. I can just say that this subject matter is regulated through 470 and 473, specifically, those rules. If necessary, I can read them out. I would like to read Rule 470, only the relevant portion pertaining to this subject matter, as well as 473.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the interpreters please have the copy placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute, please. The interpreters are asking for a copy to be placed on the ELMO. Would the usher see to that, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am quoting 470: "In addition to their regular tasks, the units and institutions of the army can be used in peacetime for the protection of people and property from natural disasters and other calamities; ensuring public communications and facilities of particular importance for the defence of the country; keeping law and order at big celebrations and parades; struggle against renegades, sabotage, terrorists, and other hostile or enemy armed groups; preventing and eliminating an emergency situation." So I referred to one subparagraph which is further elaborated in 473. And 473 reads as following: "The units of the army can be used in the struggle against renegades, sabotage, and other hostile groups."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just to clarify the history. I've been able to find the reference to rules of service, and I did indeed refer to Article 470, and I drew that reference at that stage from the witness's thesis that I had read. And I explained to him that I was reading it -- I was quoting it from his own thesis to him. Now, whether we've got the original rules of service in full as part of Mr. Coo's report, we're checking, and we'll have a result, I hope, by the end of the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Milosevic, a question now on the rules. The witness has read the relevant sections.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I haven't finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Okay, then.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He didn't manage to finish the next article, because Mr. Nice interrupted.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation]: "i.e., to prevent and eliminate a state of emergency according to the decision of the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, or rather, the Supreme Defence Council. In order to use the units of the army, in order to carry out the tasks from this article, such an order will be issued by the chief of General Staff. When renegade, terrorist, sabotage and other enemy armed groups attack a unit or institution, the commander --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Milosevic please wait for the interpretation to finish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the interpreters are asking you to wait for the interpretation to finish; in other words, to observe the pause between answer and question.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note that the General was reading the text very fast.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, is it correct what General Perisic mentioned in his letter, that the army cannot be used before a state of emergency is proclaimed, or is that not true?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is absolutely not true. And any professional soldier knows that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. General, I have the reference here.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, tab 628.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You explained the chain of command of the army of Yugoslavia, the 3rd Army, the Pristina Corps, and your brigade. Could you please explain from that tab the organisational structure of the reinforcements of the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a schematic here of the organisational structure of the Pristina Corps in peacetime and in wartime. You referred to reinforcements, and reinforcements relate only to a state of war. So then I explained only that schematic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Only that schematic.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The corps is headed by its commander. He has his staff that is commanded by his deputy, or rather, the Chief of Staff. It includes the command, the electronic surveillance company, the squad for communication with aircraft. Then there is the next one, the department for information and psychological and propaganda activities, headed by his assistant commander for morale. The military orchestra is linked to that, and also another unit that exists only in war. Then there is the department for security, which is headed by his assistant commander for security, and the 52nd Battalion of the Military Police is directly linked to that. Then there is the organ for legal matters and to it are linked the military court and the military prosecutor. Then there is a sector for personnel, headed by his assistant commander for personnel, and then there is the organ for logistics. As for subordinated units, the Pristina Corps had its brigades, namely, the 78th Motorised Brigade. I think it's not necessary for me to read out all its three motorised battalions and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think we are looking at page 13 of that document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Serbian version is page 9. So all the motorised brigades have the same composition, three motorised battalions, an armoured battalion, a howitzer division, 122-millimetres, a mixed anti-armour division, an artillery battalion of the PVO, an engineering battalion, and a logistics battalion. That's the kind of structure that the 125th Motorised Brigade has, my brigade, the 549th Brigade, while the 354th Infantry Brigade has a different structure. Three infantry battalions, the 354th detachment, a howitzer division, a 105 millimetres --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Presiding Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, where are we heading with this? Where are we going?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll explain it to you very briefly now. I wanted General Delic to explain all the reinforcements of the Pristina Corps. I want to put a question to him: Whether this diagram contains all the reinforcements of the Pristina Corps, that is to say, all reinforcements that could have been present in Kosovo and Metohija. That is the answer I was looking for. Then I want to ask about statements made by a Prosecution witness, or rather, Mr. Nice's witness, about certain formations that were not contained in this diagram. I wanted the witness to explain that to me. So I want to refute the assertions made by the other side. I didn't want to put a leading question to him, so I asked him to mention all the reinforcements of the Pristina Corps here. However, since you've asked me what I intend to do with that, I have to say what I'm going to do with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll come to that after the break. We'll break now for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: A couple of administrative matters. The photographs provided this morning have no accompanying explanatory statement and are effectively not capable of sensible interpretation, either as to why particular positions have been chosen for apparent lines of sight or what is revealed. And of course, there's no explanation as to who conducted the exercise, and so on. Without prejudice to the fact that I would object to the production of material of this kind through this witness in re-examination, if the accused has an explanatory statement and he wants me to look at it, I will do my best to find the time and the resources to do so this afternoon. But as it is, it's just maps that really we can't deal with as they stand. The second point, separate from the first, relates to rules of service. No, we don't have the document. It was referred to only in the thesis. The Chamber may recall that the cross-examination in respect of rules of service was to the effect not accepted at full value by this witness, that they were a secret document signed by this accused and issues between the Prosecution and the Defence may in due course include whether these so-called rules of service had any constitutional power when measured against the constitution which limited the authority to use the army other than in a state of emergency or in time of war. So that we don't have them. They haven't been produced by the accused, although they were relied on and referred to by him in evidence in chief. So if he wants them before the Chamber, he's going to have to do something about it, or we may do something about it. But in any event, their constitutional position may be the necessary subject of further evidence. Finally, the documents I referred to before the witness came in this morning are being looked at at the moment, and I expect that whatever other application I may make, I will want to ask some questions at the very least arising from what I will know of those documents by tomorrow morning, with the Chamber's leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Milosevic, can you provide information about the documents that you just passed on before the break by way of explanation? Indeed, that would be helpful and relevant in relation to the issue of admissibility.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness says he doesn't know what's on these maps, or rather, Mr. Nice says he doesn't know what's on these maps. Each one of those 3-D presentations has a title. I just gave them to the witness, so I don't have them before me anymore. But on most of those photographs, they were prepared by the military geographical institute. So by professional geographers who were able to make these photographs and who are able indeed to provide a 3-D picture of every part of the terrain. And they can withstand verification by any expert. If Mr. Nice doubts it, he can get additional expertise. Secondly, below every photograph there is a diagram showing differences in altitude and the line drawn by these differences in altitude. And where these lines are interrupted. So we can easily see whether, from that point shown on the photograph, you can see another point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milosevic. We will look at that issue tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have another question, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Mr. Robinson. Mr. Nice mentioned some sort of secret document that I signed, allegedly. Since I don't know what that could be, and Mr. Nice seems to know, I would like to have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is this? What document is this?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This was explained by cross-examination through the witness to the accused, had he been attending. The rules of service on which this witness has relied for intervention of the army in Kosovo and civilian matters outside a state of emergency or times of war, signed by this accused. The suggestion to the witness that it was a secret document met with a response by him to the effect that it was at the lowest level of secrecy, or whatever it may be, the issue between the parties may be, or an issue between the parties may be whether this document, apparently signed by this accused, but so far not produced by him, although he got the witness to rely on it on several occasions, an issue may be whether it has any constitutional power, given the superior constitutional power of the constitution itself, which says when an army may be used. So the accused knows perfectly well what I'm talking about. If you look at the LiveNote transcript, there are a very large number of questions and answers by him and the witness on this topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Milosevic. That's the information in relation to that document. Let us proceed with the re-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I must say, Mr. Robinson, that this information means nothing to me, because I'm not aware of any secret document to which this witness referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The rules of service document that Mr. Nice is referring to.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The rules of service are not a secret document. They're just marked "not meant for publishing," but they're not a secret to any member of the army of Yugoslavia. It's not a secret document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, I asked you to describe the composition and the reinforcements of the Pristina Corps, and you were justified in describing only the part of the document that refers to wartime, because only in that situation does the corps have reinforcements. Did you finish?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I left off with this organic unit. 15th Armoured Brigade, 243rd Mechanised Brigade, 159th Anti-aircraft Unit, reinforcements, Military Police Battalion of the 1st Army. That's only one company of the military police from a battalion from the 1st Army. 252nd Armoured Brigade from the 1st Army. A Tactical Group, 252, from the 1st Army. That was in fact part of this 252nd Armoured Brigade, one battalion. 1 Motorised Brigade from the 2nd Army, 7th Infantry Brigade from the Nis Corps, which belongs to the 3rd Army, 175th Infantry Brigade from the Nis Corps, and Combat Group 211 from the Nis Corps. So the units that I just enumerated were reinforcements to the Pristina Corps. Parts from the 1st Army, parts from the 3rd Army, and only one from the 2nd Army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Nike Peraj, a Prosecution witness, testified here. I asked questions about his testimony of other witnesses, but now you. He speaks about paramilitary formations in Kosovo and Metohija and even one brigade from Republika Srpska which he says arrived with tanks. Do you know anything about that? Because that allegedly happened on your territory.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was my zone, and especially Djakovica. You know that I was born there. First of all, it was not possible for any brigade of that kind to be there, especially not from Republika Srpska. I think you asked me about that even last time. Tanks were mentioned, tanks from Republika Srpska. It is simply impossible that any unit outside what I describe right now was present on the territory of the Pristina Corps or the territory of my area of responsibility. I must say, Nike Peraj is not a professional military officer. He did not graduate from the military academy. His competencies are very limited because he practically didn't finish his higher education. He served for ten years in another area where I worked as a lecturer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is an operation that started in October/November 1998, he says, and practically ended in January or February. Since the OSCE mission was on the ground at the time monitoring all activities, and their reports don't reflect anything of the kind, is it possible that this mobilisation operation took place?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The OSCE monitoring mission knew everything, down to the last soldier, down to the last weapon, how many troops there were on the ground, including all barracks, all deployment points. So this is absolutely untrue. The first mobilisation happened in February and only related to anti-aircraft defence units. So there was no mobilisation prior to February. And even in February, only anti-aircraft defence units were mobilised.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were familiar with the methods of work of the OSCE mission and you were in contact with them. Would they notice this mobilisation that Peraj refers to or could it have passed unnoticed by them?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was frequently in contact with the head of the Operations Centre 1, Mazovjev [phoen], I think his name was. And six of my officers had the exclusive job of maintaining daily contacts with the mission. If you want me to tell you what it looked like in practice, I will. Every day, in front of my barracks, that has two entrances, at the front and at the rear, there were yellow OSCE vehicles observing the barracks and monitoring all entry and exit. If one vehicle should leave the barracks, that vehicle was followed, to see where it was going. And you can see from all the documents in my tabs that we had the obligation to notify to the mission in advance every departure, every movement, even if it only concerned a soldier who was going on leave. And if you want me, I can find a specific document in one of my tabs to give you an example.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it necessary to give a specific example, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This same witness, Peraj, claims in his statement that in the area Djakovica there were over 170 tanks and that there were ten tanks in Djakovica that belonged to your brigade. Is this correct? And if so, why so many tanks in the area of Djakovica?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In which period, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the war, General.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My brigade has a total of 31 combat tanks. It's a motorised brigade and has 31 combat tanks. The next one, 125th Brigade, based in Kosovska Mitrovica, had an armoured battalion in Djakovica, and they too had 31 combat tanks. 243rd Mechanised Brigade had about 60 or maybe 63 tanks. And the 15th Armoured Brigade from Pristina had the same amount of tanks. That means that even if we had assembled all the tanks that existed in the Pristina Corps and put them in Djakovica, we wouldn't have the number the witness claims we had. Secondly, following orders from the command of the corps, three of my tanks had to be placed in the platoon in Duzine village, west of Djakovica. I can show you on the map. And the orders also stipulated that another three tanks had to be in another barracks of my battalion, in Djakovica. That's a total of six. Three tanks from the 125th Brigade were in Ponosevac and three were in Junik. In end 1998, my tanks were pulled back to Prizren, into my combat group. So that at the beginning of the war, the closest of my tanks facing Djakovica were in the area of Kusni Has village. That is south-east of Djakovica, at a distance of 10 to 12 kilometres. So none of them were in the area of Djakovica. To cut a long story short, what this witness says about tanks is pure invention.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He says that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We're spending quite a lot of time on this. I've been a little bit concerned from the beginning to know how exactly it arises from cross-examination. I'm not sure whether it does or it doesn't. I've always been trying to find out what degree the accused putting up a straw man to knock down, i.e., to what degree what is said about the deployment of tanks is actually different in substance from what the witness Nike Peraj said. I'm not sure that this is proper matter for re-examination, but it's taken a great deal of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I agree. I'm not sure whether it arises, Mr. Milosevic, but you have spent enough time on it. So move on to another question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My next question has to do with mobilisation. The same witness, Peraj, claims that mobilisation was handled for the army of Yugoslavia by a certain person M. The rest is unintelligible.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: To what issue in cross-examination is this next passage of questioning going to relate?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Answer that question, Mr. Milosevic. To what issue in cross-examination does this relate?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nice questioned the witness about the forces available to the brigade headed by the witness, commanded by the witness, and that's in relation to this demand made by Mr. Nice. And he was the one who put witness Nike Peraj on the stand to testify in favour of his case, and I think this questioning is absolutely justified. This testimony does relate to the area of responsibility of Mr. Delic. That is not in dispute. And courtesy of my liaison officer, I also have the statement of witness Nike Peraj where all the passages quoted in my questions are contained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Which witness is he talking about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I remember Mr. Nice put several questions in relation to Mr. Peraj but I'm not sure whether this topic specifically was raised or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Neither am I, Your Honour. My microphone is not working. Neither am I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Milosevic. Deal with it briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, we were talking about the mobilisation. Could you explain who effected the mobilisation for your unit?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For my unit, the mobilisation was carried out by the military department of Prizren and Leskovac. So for part of the reserve force from the territory of the Prizren municipality, Orahovac and Suva Reka, it was done by the Prizren department, with its branch offices in these places. And for the reservists, to replenish the Leskovac municipality Lebane and so on, it was the Leskovac military department which was in charge of that. And the military departments are linked to the military districts. That is common knowledge. And in actual fact, they were within the army system. Nobody from outside could have conducted the mobilisation, not only for the purposes of my own unit, but for any other unit either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, did you happen to know General Micunovic who worked in the military department? Do you know why he was arrested at the beginning of May?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know Major Micunovic. He was from Djakovica, the village of Korenica, in fact. I knew him personally. We didn't see each other often. He was the commander of the 53rd Border Battalion at one point and after that he worked in the military department. And during the war, during the war he was the commander of the 113th Military Territorial Detachment from Djakovica. And a company of that detachment was attached to my own brigade. So that I do know him, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Nike Peraj said that Micunovic engaged in impermissible actions or business. Is that true or not?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean. What impermissible business? I don't know anything about that. All I do know is something quite different linked directly to the service and the performance of his duties. I don't know what Nike Peraj had in mind specifically when he said that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Nike Peraj said that Micunovic was arrested at his paragraph 52 of his statement. He stayed there just three days, and that he heard about the arrest from his brother. He was an army -- soldier in the army of Yugoslavia. And that Micunovic allegedly was released, thanks to the personal intervention of Seselj and Arkan.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's to say the least quite ridiculous. Micunovic was replaced from his duties as commander of the military territorial detachment. I think it was sometime in mid-April. And he was replaced because he did not provide security for the unit. Because he did not invest sufficient effort in seeing that his unit was entrenched in its defence area. And he wasn't arrested, and he was placed at the disposal, as far as I can remember, of the forward command post of the Pristina Corps in Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I just wanted to hear that this wasn't correct either, what this witness testified to as before. And this witness says that it left the Djakovica area before the NATO attack and that it planned its operations from Albania?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I am sure that -- I'm almost certain I asked not a single question about Micunovic of this witness or this part of Peraj's evidence, which comes incidentally, to remind us, in the form of 92 bis statement with cross-examination allowed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Move on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the problem really is that at the end of the whole case, if we have large passages of re-examination that should have been led as examination-in-chief and thus signalled for possible cross-examination, but there's been no cross-examination, probably the evidence is valueless because it's never been tested. And this is one of the real problems. Whether we can ever distinguish what is and what isn't properly within re-examination of a particular witness is uncertain, but it would be a huge exercise, in light of the way the accused does it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the re-examination is, of course, as you know, confined to matters arising from cross-examination. Mr. Nice may, in cross-examination, refer to a particular Prosecution witness, but that doesn't let in, in re-examination, all of that witness's evidence. It only would let in that part which was referred to in cross-examination. So let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, during the cross-examination, you mentioned direct cooperation between the KLA and NATO, and in addition to your personal experience, you provided certain documents, in tabs, let me see, 620 to 623 inclusive. Is that so? And would you like to add anything on the subject, any other evidence and proof confirming that collaboration?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, this is a matter in which I am interested. During cross-examination, as you say, he mentioned direct cooperation between the KLA and NATO. And you're now asking him for additional -- any additional information he has on that. But to what end? For what purpose? And how does it arise? It's something that has already been dealt with. The witness has already given evidence on it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I will just focus, then, on the question raised by Mr. Bonomy as to whether in this operation, in addition to air support, there was the participation of ground forces belonging to American units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What can you say about that, and have you heard of the Atlantic Brigade, so-called?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember that Mr. Bonomy was particularly interested in hearing about, in addition to the air campaign, whether there was any ground campaign afoot. There was direct cooperation, there was direct cooperation and operations on the part of a strong unit, an operative group called Jastreb which had radars for the detection of our artillery, and it was preparing goals for the air force and helicopters and provided that information to the KLA, and he speaks about that on a number of pages, or rather, Mr. Wesley Clark writes about that. And as far as the unit you mention, the Atlantic Brigade, there's a whole book written about it. It was a unit which was composed of Albanians who were born in America.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you mean Americans of Albanian descent or origin, is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Albanians who had established that unit in America. In the month of April they arrived, and that's what it says in the book. They arrived in April, on the territory of Albania, that is, where they received all their equipment and weapons. And they participated in this last operation, the Strela, or Arrow Operation. After that, they reached Pristina, and they were demobilised there and then they went back to America. So that is the Atlantic Brigade that is mentioned. It's mentioned in several places. And they had -- they were well armed and they had American --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What was the strength of this unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it was about 400 men, 400 men-strong, approximately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Both of the Jastreb Unit and the Atlantic Brigade, you would be unaware of at the time the events were occurring.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter's note Jastreb Unit being Hawk Unit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as the Atlantic Brigade was concerned, we knew about it. As far as the hawk group, or Jastreb, we Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. didn't know that was its name, but we did know that a unit was in existence which followed our connections and the work of our artillery. So it was a unit with radar to detect artillery. We didn't know that its name was Hawk, the Hawk Operative Group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Where did you engage the Atlantic Brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the Atlantic Brigade, you have it mentioned in a number of places.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Where did you encounter them? Where did you engage in combat with them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was the battle at Mount Pastrik, within the framework of the Arrow Operation, or Strela, in translation, from the 26th of May up until around the 9th of June.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And who were they fighting with? Who were they assisting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Directly with -- well, they were directly with the KLA, and they were fighting against my unit. That means that that unit was along my axis, on Mount Pastrik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm now confused. I thought this was a unit of 400 people that was identifiable. But are you now saying they're simply mixed with KLA terrorists?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, they weren't mixed with them. They were a unit that was completely separate from the KLA. But they had on one shoulder the American flag and on the other shoulder the KLA insignia. So they were American citizens of Albanian origin. And if you would like me read out to you several sentences written by a member of that brigade, and he wrote something in his book when he returned to America.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I really wanted to know what your personal knowledge of them was, and I thought that's the basis on which you were answering.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, my knowledge is that that unit fought directly against me, against my unit. So Pastrik wasn't an area where I was not; it was where I was. I was constantly in my unit fighting on Mount Pastrik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I thought that's how you were trying to answer, and then when you referred to books -- I'm not really particularly interested in your knowledge gained by books. I'm interested in what I thought you were telling me, which was your own personal experience. And that's why I would rather confine my inquiry to what you personally know. And I understood you to be telling me that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that time, I didn't know how many of them there were. I learnt their numbers from reading the book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Delic, did you say that they participated under the American flag in the Arrow Operation from the 26th of May to the 9th of June? Is that what you said a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They took part under the American flag and they had the American flag on their uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that operation stood from the 26th of May, 1999; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. From the 26th of May until the 9th of June, to the end. But the intensity of the fighting after the 5th of June abated. The worst battles went on on the 27th, 28th, and 29th of May, as well as the 30th and 31st, right up until somewhere around the 5th of June.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And what depth had they reached in our territory?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in view of the fact that it was a surprise attack on their part, they managed to penetrate to within a depth of one kilometre, along one axis, perhaps a little more than a kilometre in some areas. In other areas it was just 500 metres in depth. But after two days, we managed to push them out, all these forces, outside, we pushed them out of our territory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Jamie Shea spoke about that, about those battles and that fighting, and that in the course of one day, for instance, one whole battalion was destroyed, numbering about 800 soldiers, and that the KLA forces had succeeded in arriving at the immediate vicinity of Prizren, to the left banks of the Dim [phoen] River.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that wasn't true, was it? It wasn't correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, none of that was correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Now, General, Mr. Nice, on several occasions, asked questions linked to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
